1269-the-soul-of-a-bishop:
H. G. Wells tells of a bishop of the Church of England who, worn by war and doubt, loses faith in the creeds he preaches and seeks a simpler, more living God. The novel follows his crisis through sermons, family strife, and a vision that remakes his ministry.

Wells uses the bishop to argue his own religious ideas, much as in God the Invisible King, but here in story form. The prose is earnest and direct. The book gives a window on wartime faith and doubt, and it draws readers who like novels of ideas.
15899-susan-clegg-and-her-friend-mrs-lat:
A comic novel by Anne Warner, author of A Woman's Will, issued by Little, Brown, and Company in Boston in 1904. The first four chapters appeared as separate stories in The Century Magazine during the past year, revised for book publication. The Minister's Vacation, never before printed, was added. Warner notes that Miss Clegg, Mrs. Lathrop, and the other characters are inventions.

Susan Clegg, a sharp-tongued New England spinster, spars with her friend Mrs. Lathrop over neighbours, ministers, and morals. Gossip, letters, and village doings fill the chapters. Warner writes in dialect with a keen comic ear. The book delights as a village comedy: two old friends, talking their way through life's small wars.
16925-sally-bishop:
E. Temple Thurston wrote this romance, new cheaper edition issued by Chapman and Hall in London in 1912, with American copyright in 1909. Thurston dedicates it to Gerald du Maurier and defends his subtitle, a romance, against critics who demand that a romance end with happiness ever after. He notes the unwritten rule that books must close with a phrase of lasting joy.

Thurston tells of Sally Bishop, a woman caught between love and the rules of her world, in a tale that refuses easy comfort. The romance is earnest, modern for its day, and full of London life. Readers who like early 1900s novels of love and duty will find a thoughtful, well-written tale that ends on its own terms, not on a formula.
172-the-haunted-bookshop:
Roger Mifflin runs a Brooklyn bookshop where books, he claims, haunt their readers. Christopher Morley's Haunted Bookshop continues the bookseller's adventures from Parnassus on Wheels, now with a young advertising man and Titania Chapman. Love soon runs away with the tale.

A German plot, a missing book, and wartime nerves weave through the shop's shelves. Morley dedicates the book to booksellers and praises their trade throughout. Chapters first ran in The Bookman magazine. The novel remains a warm hymn to bookshops and the people who keep them. Morley's shop scenes still draw booksellers who recognize their own customers in them.
17530-maida-s-little-shop:
Inez Haynes Irwin, author of Maida's Little House and Maida's Little School, published this children's book in 1909, with copyright held by B. W. Huebsch. Maida's story continues in a little shop. The chapters follow her days in order: the ride, cleaning up, the first day, the second day, Primrose Court, two calls, trouble, a rainy day, work, and play.

Later chapters bring Halloween, the first snow, the fair, and Christmas happenings. Readers get a warm, everyday story of a girl learning to run a shop and to deal with neighbours, told in Irwin's plain, kindly style. The book suits young readers who enjoy stories of work, seasons, and small triumphs.
19809-the-story-of-a-dewdrop:
John Aikin's The Story of a Dewdrop is a small nature tale for children. Its dewdrop is a puzzle to every creature that meets it. Where it came from, nobody knows. What it is made of puzzles them more. It arrived quietly, a visitor from some unknown land. The birds, one by one, try stealthily to track its path.

Victorian nature tales taught science through wonder. A dewdrop's short life can carry evaporation, light, and weather. Aikin wrote improving books for the young with his sister Anna Barbauld. Their tradition joined fact to gentle moral feeling. The dewdrop's mystery keeps young readers asking questions. That was precisely the authors' method and aim.
19871-serbia-in-light-and-darkness-with-:
Serbia in Light and Darkness presents Serbia to British readers, with photographs. Its pictures list King Peter and a Turkish general. Serbian soldiers appear with an English nurse in several plates. Other scenes show a cattle market and peasant types. Montenegrin ladies and monastery superiors also pose. The Archbishop of Canterbury supplied a preface.

Britain and Serbia became allies in the Great War. Books like this built public sympathy for a small ally. Photographs of soldiers and women doing men's work carried the argument. The author, Father Nikolai Velimirovic, was a Serbian churchman. He lectured widely in Britain during the war. The book is wartime portrait and plea together.
20290-perley-s-reminiscences-of-sixty-ye:
Perley's Reminiscences holds sixty years of memories of Washington, the national capital. The book was sold only by subscription, as its notice warns readers. Agents were bound by contract to sell in no other way at all. Any breach of that plan trespassed on the author's copyright rights.

Benjamin Perley Poore knew Washington as a reporter and clerk for decades. His memories cover presidents, Congress, parties, and city society. Subscription books like this one reached homes far from bookshops. Readers get a gossip-rich tour of the capital across a long, changing era.
22966-toy-shop:
A strange demonstration runs Toy Shop. The demonstrator flips a switch and current surges toward his wave receptors. A lamp starts pulsing steadily. Then he eases a knob around, warning that the generator demands a delicate hand.

Powers of the whole world are in play, he claims, in a shop full of toys. That gap between the humble setting and the huge claim powers the story. Devices in such tales rarely stay toys for long. Readers get a compact piece of speculative fiction built around a showroom test, the kind where each turn of the knob raises the stakes and shortens the odds.
24530-on-the-tree-top:
Clara Doty Bates and others wrote this illustrated children's picture book, published at Boston in 1881 with pictures by F. T. Merrill, Jessie Curtis, and other artists. Each colour plate carries a short poem within the plate itself. Contents include The Gold Spinner, A Fish Story, Pussy Cat's Doings, and The Three Little Kittens.

Later pieces retell Dick Whittington and Puss in Boots, with Jack and Jill among the rhymes. The book is a handsome example of Victorian gift-book making, where verse and picture share the page. Young readers, and collectors of old children's books, will enjoy its charm and its bright, old-fashioned art.
24834-the-wonders-of-a-toy-shop:
The Wonders of a Toy-Shop, printed in New York by J. Q. Preble, is a short verse tour of a toy warehouse. A cheerful toyman shows young visitors his stock. A menagerie holds a wide-jawed lion and a tame tiger. Wagons and drays come with horses and harness, a file of toy soldiers stands ready, and a stud of horses eats no corn. A plump coachman costs nothing to feed.

Each verse pairs with a picture, and the jokes are gentle: wonders never cease when toys cost no keep. The book keeps the look of an early American toy book, made to be read aloud at Christmas or birthdays. Young children will enjoy its parade of playthings, all ready for parlour or drawing room.
27125-the-splash-of-a-drop:
Professor A. M. Worthington's The Splash of a Drop, published in 1895, reprints his discourse delivered at the Royal Institution on May 18, 1894. Worthington argues that a splash, done in the twinkling of an eye, is an exquisitely regulated phenomenon that illustrates the fundamental properties of fluids.

Instantaneous photographs show a water drop falling about sixteen inches into milk, timed to fractions of a second after contact. Worthington also notes new work by Lenard in Germany and J. J. Thomson at Cambridge on the electrical charges that certain splashes develop. Worthington's discourse was published under the direction of the General Literature Committee. The book was printed for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge.
27907-hunting-the-skipper-the-cruise-of-:
George Manville Fenn wrote Hunting the Skipper, the cruise of the Seafowl sloop, a naval adventure opening aboard Her Majesty's ship Seafowl off the west coast of Africa. Two midshipmen, Frank Murray and his friend Dicky, peer through telescopes into a hot, thick haze.

The lads trade jokes about blue pills, jellyfish, and fevers while the sails flap in a dying wind, setting the tone for a tale of heat, duty, and pursuit at sea. Fenn, a prolific boys' author, writes with the detail of a man who loved ships and the energy of a storyteller for young readers.
29321-vulcan-s-workshop:
Harl Vincent published this story in Astounding Stories in June 1932. Luke Fenton, a great swaggering figure, reels back from a porthole cursing, his hairy paws pressed over his eyes. No one warned him that gazing at the sun's unscreened orb, only twenty million miles away, could blind him.

Fenton, the magazine says, swaggers defiantly in Vulcan's Workshop, the most frightful of Martian prisons. He knows nothing of vast distances or of airless space letting the sun's rays strike unfiltered. Readers get a pulp prison adventure on Mars, where a tough man's ignorance of space itself becomes his first enemy.
33458-the-captain-of-the-gray-horse-troo:
Hamlin Garland's Captain of the Gray-Horse Troop, in a sunset edition copyrighted in 1901 and 1902, follows a cavalry captain on the western frontier. Its chapters move from a camp in the snow and the Streeter gun-rack. Curtis takes charge, meets the beautiful Elsie Bee Bee, sees caged eagles, and seeks a truce that Elsie at last allows. Garland writes of soldiers, settlers, and Native peoples with a realist's eye.

The novel's strength lies in its western detail and its humane view of a hard frontier, where duty and love cross. Its pace is steady, its scenes vivid, and its hero, Curtis, carries the tale with quiet force. For readers of western fiction, it is a strong, thoughtful novel from a writer who knew the plains well.
37743-the-attitudes-of-animals-in-motion:
Attitudes of Animals in Motion is the text of a lecture by Eadweard Muybridge of San Francisco. He gave it at an extra evening meeting of the Royal Institution of Great Britain. The date was March thirteen, eighteen eighty two. The Prince of Wales sat in the chair. Muybridge showed his pictures with a device called the zoopraxiscope, the title says.

The problem of animal motion has engaged mankind through all history, he begins. Job describes the action of the horse, and Homer that of the ox. Aristotle gave it deep attention, and Borelli a lifetime. Marey of France, in our own day, used tubes and air chambers on a horse's shoes, he notes. Pencils recorded the steps on a turning cylinder in that system. Artists, he adds, long copied old errors without fresh inquiry.
37809-a-taxonomic-revision-of-the-leptod:
A Taxonomic Revision of the Leptodactylid Frog Genus Syrrhophus is a zoological monograph by John D Lynch. The University of Kansas Museum of Natural History published it in 1970. It forms volume twenty, number one of the museum's publications, running to forty five pages with twenty two figures.

Lynch begins with an analysis of characters. Size and proportions come first: frogs of this genus run from sixteen to forty millimetres in snout vent length. Five species are named as relatively small, among them the modestus and pallidus forms. Such revisions sort museum specimens into species by bone, toe, and voice. The genus lives in the American tropics, where tiny frogs call from leaf litter. Lynch's paper gave their tangled names a modern order, on which later field guides still rest.
38267-international-congress-of-arts-and:
The International Congress of Arts and Science gathered the world's scholars to lecture on every field of learning, and its lectures were printed in a Cambridge Edition of 750 sets. Howard Rogers, director of congresses, edited the set. This first volume holds Philosophy and Metaphysics.

A photogravure of Daniel French's statue Alma Mater, the gilded bronze at Columbia University, stands at the front. The plate note describes her: seated in a classic chair, sceptre in hand, a wreath on her head, and an open book on her lap. She figures the fostering mother of minds, the congress's own emblem. Scholars get the opening volume of a vast Edwardian stocktaking of knowledge, field by field, by the men who worked them.
38307-great-hike-or-the-pride-of-the-kha:
Alan Douglas, a scout-master, wrote this boys' book in the Hickory Ridge Boy Scouts series. The series list at the front describes camp tales full of woodcraft and outdoor skill. In one earlier book, Elmer Chenowith, a lad from the northwest woods, stuns everyone with his grasp of camp life.

A great hike stands at the center of this volume, and the khaki troop's pride rides on it. The publisher promises clean, wholesome stories that every boy should read. Campfires, patrol work and tests of skill in the open air give young readers both adventure and a model of scout conduct.
41268-manual-training-toys-for-the-boy-s:
Manual Training Toys for the Boys Workshop is a craft book by Harris Moore, a chief of hand work in a town school. It came out in nineteen twelve and is writ to the boy who likes to potter. Its front part treats the bench, the mark tools, saws, planes, bits, nails, and screws. Rules for the plane close that part.

Past fifty toy plans fill the book, each with its plate. Darts, tops, a drum, a pop gun, a bow, and a charm box lead the list. Mills, kites of three kinds, a kite string boat, and a wea house take their turns. A cart, a gun, a pile tool, and a force pump close the rows. Moore bids the boy study each draw well, since each line has a sense.
42083-chaucer-s-translation-of-boethius-:
Geoffrey Chaucer translated Boethius, De Consolatione Philosophiae, into English prose. This text rests on the Cambridge manuscript, with line notes and sidenotes kept. Skeat's edition of Chaucer's complete works is the guide named for its marks. A sign in the notes points to the Harley manuscript 2421, by that account. Line numbers follow the standard multiples of four used by the Early English Text Society.

Headnotes have been moved to the nearest convenient line break for this form. Words that expand short forms stand in braces, and other italics stand in the usual marks. A Greek phrase, follow God, stands in the sidenotes of the work. An appendix shows decorative final letters with a single cross mark. The text gives Chaucer's Boece, his Boethius in English dress, in a form made for close study of each line.
43376-the-american-language-a-preliminar:
The American Language, by H L Mencken, was printed in New York by Alfred A Knopf in 1919. The first edition ran to fifteen hundred copies, and the hosted copy is number 1434. Mencken inquires into the development of English in the United States.

An opening part treats the diverging streams of British and American speech, the academic attitude, and the views of writing men and foreign observers. Thomas Jefferson, Mencken notes, saw more than a century back that American speech would split as the people grew. Later parts treat the beginnings of American in colonial days and its characters and materials. Mencken writes with wit and a mass of examples. Readers get the classic case that American English is its own tongue.
44440-mother-nature-s-toy-shop:
Mother Nature's Toy-Shop, by Lina Beard and Adelia B Beard, was published by Charles Scribner's Sons, copyright 1918, with many illustrations by the authors. A transcriber's note warns modern readers that foxglove is very poisonous and its blossoms should not be used as fairy caps.

The presentation pictures Mother Nature keeping an open toy-shop for children, free to any child who wants its goods. She pays her little shoppers in rosier cheeks, brighter eyes, and stronger bodies, and her stock changes with each season of the year. The Beards stress that all the material, text and cuts alike, is original with them. The book tells what to find outdoors and what to do with it.
49302-sweet-clover-growing-the-crop:
A farmers' bulletin on sweet clover by H S Coe. The United States Department of Agriculture issued it in April 1917. It is Farmers' Bulletin number 797. Coe worked in the Office of Forage Crop Investigations. The Bureau of Plant Industry contributed the bulletin. Its subject is simply growing the crop well.

The opening summary gives the essentials at once. White sweet clover forms most of the acreage. The plant grows in nearly every state by 1917. No true clover matches its range of climate, Coe says. It resists drought better than alfalfa or red clover. Acid soil and missing inoculation cause most failures. Seed must germinate at seventy-five percent or better. Firm seedbeds and lime complete the recipe. A companion bulletin covers using the crop.
49617-the-good-crow-s-happy-shop:
Patten Beard wrote The Good Crow's Happy Shop, a children's craft and play book published by the Pilgrim Press of Boston in 1917. Thirteen pictures show happy things the children made in the shop. The book is dedicated to Henry Jarrett and to Caw Caw, his good play crow.

Beard's opening note tells the game behind the book. Long ago she played the crow play as a little girl. Grown up, she gave the play to Henry Jarrett, and the two now give it to other children. The chapters run the shop's year: the Good Crow and Aunt Phoebe, the magic book, the paper dolls Jimsi made. Toy furniture, valentines, and embroidery patterns follow. Scrapbooks, pin-wheels, and May baskets fill the later chapters. A Christmas tree made in the shop closes the year. Children got a workshop in a story, run by a crow.
55805-travels-in-a-tree-top:
Charles Conrad Abbott wrote Travels in a Tree Top, sold in buckram at one dollar fifty with a front print by Alice Barber Stephens and three photogravures. Front pages list Abbott's books in his Fireside and Forest Library. The Freedom of the Fields is its mate at the same price. Recent Rambles and Bird Land Echoes stand in the list too.

Abbott's nature books treat birds, fields, and woods near home. The Birds About Us and a novel named The Hermit of Nottingham hold the list. Travels in a Tree Top takes its name from close watch of life high in the branches. Two volumes in a box held the mate pair for three dollars. The tone is calm and fond, made for readers who ramble and watch with care.
56237-the-pink-shop:
The Pink Shop is a mystery novel by Fergus Hume. F V White published it in London in 1911. Hume was already famous for The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. The pink shop of the title stands in a mean lane off High Street, Kensington. Madame Coralie runs it as a Turkish Shop for beauty.

Coralie restores elderly ladies to a look of youth, with paint rather than Medea's cauldron. Her clients visit in secrecy and leave their broughams ugly, returning beautiful. The chapter titles promise a lost bag and an inquest. A lady detective appears, and the question of the clock matters. Audrey hears things she should not, and a photograph tells part of the truth. The chapters parcel the truth out in pieces. Revenge and final explanations close the book.
57122-climate-and-health-in-hot-countrie:
Giles counsels travellers in Climate and Health in Hot Countries, printed in New York in 1905. William Wood made the book. Giles served in the Indian Medical Service, retired, and had writ on gnats or mosquitoes, on kala azar, and on beri beri. The sub title calls it a popular treatise on personal hygiene in the hotter parts of the world, with the outlines of tropical climatology.

His first word recalls a darker age. A hundred years back, a long stay in the tropics was regarded with well founded horror, he says. The best the white settler dared hope for was a short life and a merry one, and the mirth was often lacking. Clive's father got his troublesome son a writership to India as a last resource, he tells, and felt he had signed the youth's doom.
57447-the-romance-of-a-shop:
Amy Levy writes of working women in The Romance of a Shop, printed at Boston in 1889. Cupples and Hurd made the book. Twenty four chapters and an epilogue carry the tale. A Tennyson tag on Fortune's wheel fronts the first chapter.

In the Beginning leads, then Friends in Need and Ways and Means. Number Twenty B names the shop itself, and This Working Day World states the theme. To the Rescue, A New Customer, and A Distinguished Person build the trade side. Show Sunday and Summing Up stand in the mid run. Gertrude is Anxious, Lucy, Cressida, and Phyllis name the women at the heart of it. In the Sick Room, The Last Act, A Dismissal, and At Last close the arc of shop and sisters.
57487-the-juggler-s-oracle-or-the-whole-:
The Juggler's Oracle, or the Whole Art of Legerdemain Laid Open, was printed in London for William Cole. Its maker, Sieur H Boaz, calls himself a teacher of the art for thirty years. More than forty wood cuts show the tricks. The title page vows to bare the newest and most strange tricks of the craft.

First come card tricks, from the pass to a card nailed to a wall by a pistol shot. Cups and balls come next, then feats with coins and rings. Later parts use fire, strings, knots, and sight tricks. Work with false cures and mixed drinks is also shown. Stage hopefuls get a full trade book of the old conjuring craft, secret by secret.
5866-yollop:
McCutcheon published Yollop in New York in 1922, with a frontispiece by Edward Caswell. A frontispiece scene leaves Mrs Champney seated alone and helpless amid confusion, while a man named Smilk marches Mr Yollop to his bedroom, setting a comic household crisis in motion. The novel that follows turns on Yollop himself, a figure whose doings stir a household to laughter and alarm.

Readers get McCutcheon's light comedy of manners, where a single eccentric character upsets servants, guests, and family plans. The humor favors situation and dialogue over plot machinery, with confusion itself as the engine. Fans of McCutcheon's popular romances will enjoy a shorter, funnier tale, and new readers will find an easy entry to his world of fashionable folly.
59559-shock-troop:
Shock Troop is a science fiction story by Richard Bolton, first printed in the magazine Worlds of If in October 1956. A headnote sets the tone. The invaders were going to make galactic history, but fate made it a comedy of errors.

Commander Zurg briefs his officers as the ship swings into orbit around the third planet. He speaks in the stylized movements of the court language, and most of his officers turn puzzled colours, unable to follow him. Only his second in command stays calm, knowing the commander will drop into the common tongue after the ceremony. The green gem of the heavens below awaits its invaders. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
61309-road-stop:
David Mason wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in January 1963. Its head note says the car was like any other on the road: automatic, self contained, and eternal. A highway stretches ruler straight toward both horizons, black and shining like a river of ink. Bright pastel buildings of Rest Stop 25 stand among green trees.

Cars shoot past in flashes of metal, but the road is busier at night. Sam is the only attendant on duty. Even at its busiest, Stop 25 needs only two human attendants. Mason sets his trap in the automation of the future highway. The empty afternoon is the story's loaded quiet.
63165-crimson-clover-growing-the-crop:
Westgate wrote Crimson Clover, Growing the Crop, as Farmers' Bulletin 550 in 1913. The Government Printing Office at Washington issued it on July 9 of that year. Westgate was the agronomist in charge of clover investigations for the Bureau of Plant Industry. His letter of transmittal sends the work up through Piper, in charge of forage-crop work. More bulletins on other phases of the crop were to follow soon.

Contents open with the history and present spread of crimson clover. Requisites for a good stand, seed bed making, and fertilizers come next. Liming soils, inoculation, and seeding get full, plain treatment. Several methods of seeding crimson clover are set out side by side. The bulletin gives farmers a short, sound guide to a crop prized for feed and soil gain.
68590-the-christmas-bishop:
Winifred Kirkland's The Christmas Bishop was published by Small, Maynard of Boston in 1913, with drawings by Morrison. A picture caption sets the mood: on Christmas night, window shades roll up like eyelids opening, on home-pictures that remind the Bishop what night it is.

Part one opens before dawn on Christmas morning. Westbury lies asleep beside its curving river, great houses, churches, college, and the new tenements all still, and the Bishop alone awake. He had been a poet once, so long ago that he has forgotten his own hymns when they sing them in church. But he keeps the poet's trick of thinking in pictures between sleep and waking. The pictures march into a poem: a storied city on two hills, silent and grey, where a Child passes, and every portal he knocks at wakes to teeming life within.
69647-indian-tales-of-the-great-ones-amo:
Indian Tales of the Great Ones among Men, Women, and Bird-People, by Cornelia Sorabji, holds pictures by Warwick Goble. Sorabji gives the book to her baby friends in all worlds. Nineteen short tales draw on the old epics and past of India, told for young readers.

Two great brother eagles open the book, Jattayu, king of all the eagle tribes, and small Sanpati. They live on a crag of the Home of Snow, the peaks at the north east edge of India. Jattayu longs to fly as near the sun as he can. Sanpati finds a way, to fly above him and shield him from its blaze. More tales treat Draupadi, Raziya, queen of Delhi, and Baber the Tiger. One treats a king who kept his word. Young readers get brave, tender tales of beasts, queens, and kings.
69730-death-comes-for-the-archbishop:
Willa Cather wrote a novel printed at New York in 1927. Auspice Maria stands at the front, with Father Vaillant's signet ring pictured. Cather's shelf of O Pioneers, The Song of the Lark, and My Antonia is listed. A prologue at Rome opens the book. One summer evening in the year 1848, three cardinals and a missionary bishop from America were dining together in the gardens of a villa in the Sabine hills.

The villa was famous for the fine view from its terrace. The hidden garden where the four men sat lay some twenty feet below the terrace end, a mere shelf of rock overhanging a steep slope of vineyards. The vicar apostolic, missionary journeys, and the mass at Acoma follow. The great diocese, gold under Pike's Peak, and death coming for the archbishop close a New Mexico life. Cather builds the Southwest in still, bright prose.
700-the-old-curiosity-shop:
Charles Dickens wrote this novel about Little Nell, a girl who lives with her grandfather in his London shop of old curios. When the grandfather's gambling debts fall into the hands of the dwarf Quilp, the pair flee into the English countryside, pursued by danger and debt. Friends and foes cross their path on the road.

Nell's goodness and Quilp's malice drive a tale of flight, kindness, and loss that moved Victorian readers to tears. Dickens fills the road with vivid folk: showmen, schoolmasters, and kind strangers. The novel's fame rests on Nell herself, one of his most loved figures, and on a story that turns a child's journey into a moral fable.
72746-uncle-wiggily-s-rolling-hoop:
Uncle Wiggily's Rolling Hoop is a picture book for children with text by Howard R Garis and pictures by Lang Campbell, printed at Newark in 1919. It holds three stories: how the bunny gentleman gets mixed up with his rolling hoop, Uncle Wiggily and the snappy shark, and Uncle Wiggily's bob sled. Every book in the series has three stories, including the title story.

The front matter lists more than two dozen companion books, from Uncle Wiggily's Auto Sled to Uncle Wiggily and the Turkey Gobbler. The publisher promises that if the spoon holder does not go down cellar and take the coal shovel away from the gas stove, the reader may read them all. A bookplate verse asks the child who has read and laughed with glee to bring the book back.
75095-the-radio-cop:
Vic Whitman wrote this crime tale of a police radio announcer in a city studio. Gangdom challenges is the heading of the first chapter of the story. Patrolman Jennings, who claimed a flair for poetry, describes the hero in a verse at the start.

Dave Cates, official announcer for the police division of station KYK, had a splendid voice. Small and ready to fight at a nod was officer Cates of the wave-length squad, the verse goes on. Cates talks into the microphone over the studio as the tale opens, sending orders on new uniforms out to men who may be crooks listening in.
77070-the-mid-of-the-maintop:
Arthur Lee Knight wrote The Mid of the Maintop, a sea tale with pen and ink pictures by Hilda Robinson. The Forte, a fifty-gun frigate, works the east coast of Africa against the slave trade. Captain Brooke commands, with Commander Hutton as his second.

Jack Villiers, a smart midshipman, leads the maintopmen aloft and is a favorite with all hands. The tale opens in fog and a rising blow off Ras Hafoon, after a call at Zanzibar. Orders send the ship hunting slave dhows along the coast. Storm, chase, and fight make the young officer's life.
78288-under-the-big-top:
Under the Big Top is a book about the circus by Courtney Ryley Cooper. Little, Brown of Boston published it in 1924, from pieces copyrighted over four years. Scotty, a circus woman, and Grit, the lion she adopted, form the frontispiece. Cooper writes from inside the travelling show world he describes.

The why of the circus opens the chapters, and press agents follow. Entering the menagerie brings the reader among the animals in earnest. Our friends the elephants earn a chapter of their own. When the animals escape, and mothers of the menagerie, come next. In the steel arena treats the cage acts and their daily danger. The circus man's best friend and the children of the big tops follow. The show must go on is the closing chapter's famous motto.
78973-the-children-s-kraft-shop:
Adelia Beard invented, wrote and illustrated this craft book, published by Donohue at Chicago in 1914. A foreword to mothers introduces the Children's Kraftshop at the front of the volume. A new and useful field of simple handicrafts for little folk is the aim, that foreword states in its first lines.

Original toys and a new line of materials to make them are promised to children there. Paper, scissors and paste build sailboats and playthings in Beard's shop of projects. Beard, who helped found the Girl Scouts' handicraft tradition, writes so a child alone at a table can finish each toy and call it truly made.
britannica-1911-abbot-george-archbishop:
George Abbot, archbishop of Canterbury, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbot, a Guildford cloth-worker's son born in 1562, rose at Oxford to master of University College and dean of Winchester. Work on the authorized New Testament and a Scottish church mission won James the First's favor.

Lichfield, London, and Canterbury followed in quick steps by 1611. Puritan leanings set him against Catholics and court alike: he fought the Essex divorce and banned the Sunday sports declaration at Croydon. A hunting accident in 1622, when his bolt killed a keeper, shadowed his name despite a royal pardon. Charles stripped his powers after he refused a forced-loan sermon, and Laud rose as he retired. He died in 1633.
britannica-1911-adalbert-archbishop:
Adalbert (about 1000-1072) was a German archbishop. Adam of Bremen judged him the century's most famous churchman. A Saxon noble's son, he rose at Halberstadt to provost. King Henry III noticed his ability early. Adalbert likely served as chancellor for Italy. In 1045 he became archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen. His province included the Scandinavian countries. It also covered much of North Germany.

Ambition drove his northern project. He sent missionaries to Finland and Greenland. Orkney received his missions as well. He aimed to make Bremen a patriarchate. Twelve suffragan bishoprics would stand under it. Power made enemies of Saxon dukes. He governed Germany during Henry IV's minority. Opposition forced his removal from court in 1066. Recalled in 1069, he tried again and failed.
britannica-1911-adalbert-bishop:
Adalbert, born Voytech (about 950-997), is known as apostle of the Prussians. He was a Bohemian prince's son, born at Libice. Magdeburg's monastery gave him his education. In 983 he was chosen bishop of Prague. His rule proved extremely severe there. Bohemians clung to their national customs. They also kept many pagan rites. Adalbert strove in vain against both.

Failure drove him twice to Rome. The pope ordered him back in 993. Little amendment met him among his people. Papal permission then freed him for missions. He preached chiefly in North Germany and Poland. In Pomerania a heathen priest assassinated him. That martyrdom came in the year 997. Voigt's exhaustive monograph anchors the entry's sources.
britannica-1911-aesop:
Aesop is famed as the teller of fables that bear his name to this day. The 1911 Britannica entry puts his life at about 620 to 560 years before Christ. No one knows for sure where he was born at all. Thrace, Phrygia, Ethiopia, Samos, Athens, and Sardis all claim that honour. Firm facts on his life are few and hard to trust.

What is told says he was the slave of Iadmon of Samos. He met a violent death at the hands of men of Delphi. A plague that came next was blamed on that crime by many. Herodotus is the chief old source for these spare facts. Later tales give mixed and doubtful grounds for his death.
britannica-1911-aidan-bishop:
Aidan became first bishop of Lindisfarne after King Oswald asked for help in bringing back the Christian faith to Northumbria. A monk of Hii, or Iona, he was sent by Abbot Senegi in 634 or 635. True to Irish practice, he set his see on the island of Lindisfarne, near the royal centre of Bamborough.

One point set him apart from Rome: he kept the Irish day for Easter. Yet Honorius and Felix, leaders of the Roman practice, still held him in honour, won over by his character and his drive as a missionary. He lived past Oswald, his patron and friend. Aidan died on the last day of August 651, in the seventeenth year as bishop, soon after the killing of Oswine of Deira, a second friend. Bede's church history stands as the named source.
britannica-1911-benedict-biscop:
Benedict Biscop (about 628–690), also called Biscop Baducing, was an English churchman of a good Northumbrian family. He served for a time as thegn to King Oswiu, then went abroad and lived as a monk at Lerins from 665 to 667. Five journeys to Rome shaped his life’s work.

Benedict brought Theodore of Tarsus from Rome to Canterbury in 669 and became abbot of St Peter’s there. In 674 he built St Peter’s monastery at Wearmouth on land from King Ecgfrith, stocking it with a fine library. A sister house, St Paul’s at Jarrow, followed in 682. Saxon building owes nearly all to his lead, and Bede was among his pupils.
britannica-1911-bishop:
Bishop, from the Greek episkopos, meaning overseer, is a high office in certain Christian churches. A bishop is consecrated for set spiritual duties and exercises oversight over the lower clergy. In the Catholic Church bishops stand at the head of the priestly hierarchy. The 1911 Britannica article treats the office at great length and in legal detail. Whether bishops form a separate order, or only a higher grade of priest, is left a long-divided question.

The Roman Catholic section fills much of the article. A bishop there must be thirty years old, of legitimate birth, and of approved learning and virtue, under Trent's decree. Nomination shifts by country, from royal nomination to chapter election to papal choice. A double examination tests each candidate before confirmation by the Holy See. Consecration follows within three months, with laying on of hands and anointing. Other churches' practice is surveyed after the Roman model.
britannica-1911-bucketshop:
Bucketshop is a slang term from the world of finance. It names a low class of stockbroking office. This 1911 Britannica entry defines the practice. Such a broker belongs to no official exchange. He runs speculative deals for his clients. The clients put down a margin, or cover.

In most cases no real trade takes place. The deal is a simple bet between broker and client. No actual shares are bought or sold. The term is sometimes used more loosely. It then covers all brokers outside the local exchange. The entry calls that wider use wrong. The word itself is American in origin. It seems to have arisen in Chicago. The Board of Trade there banned small grain options. An unauthorized exchange opened nearby for small gamblers. Its nickname came from the “bucketful” of small speculators. They were fetched up by lift when business was slack.
britannica-1911-butler-samuel-bishop:
Samuel Butler is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English scholar and bishop born at Kenilworth in seventeen seventy four. He shone at Rugby school and then at a Cambridge college. Prize medals and grants fell to him in Greek and Latin verse.

The entry tells how he became head of a great school at Shrewsbury. He held church livings and posts while he kept that school post. For close to forty years his name was tied to the fame of that school. In his last years he rose to bishop of Lichfield in the church. He died in eighteen thirty nine with his school work still his chief mark.
britannica-1911-clarke-marcus-andrew-his:
Clarke, Marcus Andrew Hislop is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Australian author. He was born in London on the twenty-fourth of April 1846 and died in 1881. He was the only son of a barrister who died in 1863. The young man then sailed for Australia at once.

An uncle there was a county court judge. Clarke first worked as a clerk in the Bank of Australasia, but showed no gift for business. He went to learn farming on a station by the Wimmera River. He was already writing tales for magazines when, in 1867, he joined the staff of the Melbourne Argus. He later served the Melbourne public library as secretary and then as assistant librarian. His best-known book is For the Term of his Natural Life, a strong tale of a penal settlement.
britannica-1911-cooper-thomas-bishop:
Thomas Cooper (about 1517–1594), also spelled Couper, was an English bishop and writer born in Oxford. He was schooled at Magdalen College and became master of its school. He then practised as a physician in Oxford for a time. His work with books began in 1548. That year he edited a Latin dictionary, the Bibliotheca Eliotae.

In 1549 he issued a continuation of Lanquet's Chronicle of the World. Men call that work Cooper's Chronicle, and it ran through fresh editions. His greatest work came in 1565. The Thesaurus, a dictionary of Latin and English, pleased Queen Elizabeth much. Its author rose in the church from that point. He became dean of Christ Church in 1567 and dean of Gloucester in 1569. Lincoln made him bishop in 1571 and Winchester in 1584. He fought hard in print for the church against its foes.
britannica-1911-crop:
Crop is a word of Teutonic stock, kin to the German Kropf, for a swelling, a round head, or the top of anything. Its first sense is the pouched swelling of a bird's gullet, the ingluvies, where food rests for a first digestion. From the sense of top or head of a plant comes the common farming use. Crops are the produce of cultivated plants. White-crops whiten as they ripen, and green-crops do not.

In leather-dressing a crop is the whole untrimmed hide, and in mining it is the outcrop of a vein at the surface. A hunting-crop is the short thick stock of a whip, fitted with a loop for a thong. From the verb, to cut off the top, comes crop for a closely cut head of hair. That sense named the croppies, down to the Irish rebels of 1798.
britannica-1911-fauchet-claude-bishop:
Claude Fauchet (1744-1793), French revolutionary bishop, was born at Dornes in the Nievre on 22 September 1744. He served as curate of St Roch in Paris, tutored the children of the marquis of Choiseul, and rose to grand vicar of Bourges, preacher to the king and abbot. His philosophic sermons cost him his court place in 1788, and he became a popular speaker in the Paris sections.

Fauchet helped lead the attack on the Bastille and preached a funeral sermon for those killed on 14 July 1789. He ran a Social Club of the Friends of Truth, became constitutional bishop of Calvados in 1791, and sat in the Legislative Assembly and the Convention. At the king's trial he voted for appeal to the people and for imprisonment. Accused with the Girondists, he was guillotined on 31 October 1793.
britannica-1911-fulk-archbishop:
Fulk (died 900), archbishop of Reims, was elected to the see in 883 on the death of Hincmar. He fought the Normans who invaded his lands in 887. When Charles the Fat was deposed, Fulk backed Charles the Simple against Count Odo of Paris. In 893 he crowned Charles in his own church at Reims. Most nobles had then gone over to Odo.

On Odo death, Fulk won recognition of Charles from most of the nobility. In 892 he gained privileges for his province from Pope Formosus, guarding the revenues of the see during a vacancy. From 898 he also held the chancellorship, long afterwards tied to Reims. His fight to keep rich abbeys out of noble hands earned him the hatred of Baldwin, count of Flanders. Baldwin had him murdered on 17 June 900, and the weak king left the crime unpunished.
britannica-1911-gerard-archbishop:
Gerard (d. 1108) was archbishop of York under Henry I. He began his career as a clerk in the chancery of William Rufus. In 1095 he was one of two envoys sent to talk Urban II into sending a legate to England. The legate did not meet the king's hopes. Yet Gerard was paid for his work with the see of Hereford in 1096. On the death of Rufus he declared for Henry I at once.

Henry named Gerard to the see of York. Gerard balked when he was asked to make the due vow of obedience to Anselm. He took the king's side in the fight over investitures, in part, it may be, to raise the weight of his own see. He pled Henry's cause at Rome with great skill.
britannica-1911-glossop:
Glossop, a market town in Derbyshire in England, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on the far northern edge of the county, thirteen miles east of Manchester by rail. Its people numbered 21,526 in 1901. The town falls into three main parts: the Old Town, Howard Town, and Mill Town.

The article calls it the chief seat of cotton making in Derbyshire. It also had woollen and paper mills, dye and print works, and grounds for bleaching cloth. A fine church of All Saints replaced an older one in 1830, and a grand Catholic church stood in the town. Near it rose Glossop Hall, the seat of the lord of the manor, with terraced gardens. A Roman fort site guarded the dale, and five lakes to the north fed the water supply of Manchester.
britannica-1911-king-edward-bishop:
Edward King, an English bishop who lived from 1829 to 1910, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Oriel College, Oxford, and was ordained in 1854. Four years later he joined Cuddesdon College as chaplain and tutor. He was head of that college from 1863 to 1873, then a chair holder at Oxford.

King became bishop of Lincoln in 1885 and held the see until his death. His chief trial came in the years 1888 to 1890, when he was charged for acts of ritual in church. He bowed to the ruling that went against him and gave all his strength to his see. The text stresses his charm, his frank faith, and the love he won from all ranks.
britannica-1911-percy-thomas-bishop:
Thomas Percy, bishop of Dromore and editor of the Percy Reliques, was born at Bridgnorth in seventeen twenty nine. His father was a grocer of means enough to send him to Oxford. He entered Christ Church in seventeen forty six and graduated four years later. In seventeen fifty three he took the vicarage of Easton Maudit in Northamptonshire. Three years later he added a rectory in the same county.

Percy held both posts until seventeen eighty two, doing his famed literary work at Easton Maudit. There the Reliques, his great store of old ballads, was completed. Fame made him chaplain to the duke and duchess of Northumberland. He came to think he belonged to that great house himself. Through his patron he became dean of Carlisle and then bishop of Dromore. He lived, blind but sound, until September eighteen eleven.
britannica-1911-perekop:
Perekop is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Russia in the Taurida province. It stands on the neck of land that joins Crimea. That neck links the Crimea with the mainland shore. A ditch and dike of defence cross at that point. They run from the Black Sea to a salt lagoon. The town count was about five thousand souls.

Salt trade once made the town a place of weight. Salt came from salt lakes close by the town. A new rail route cut that trade away in time. The town then fell into a long decline. In Greek times a ditch gave a town there its name. Tatar khans built a fort and a new ditch in the 1400s. That fort formed the core of the town of today. Russian troops took the town more than once in the 1700s.
britannica-1911-sloop:
A sloop is a small sailing vessel with one mast, and a nautical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its rig. The mast is rigged fore and aft, in the phrase of sailors. The sails carried are a mainsail, a gaff topsail, a jib, and a fore staysail. Little in rig parts a sloop from a cutter, the entry says.

The two terms are often used without distinction between them. Some draw a line by the bowsprit, fixed in a sloop and running in a cutter. In the sailing and early steam navy, a sloop meant something else. It was a small corvette, ship rigged, with all its guns on the upper deck. The word itself was borrowed from the Dutch sloep, a boat. Kindred words live in French, Spanish, and Italian for a light boat.
britannica-1911-snowdrop:
The snowdrop, known in science as Galanthus nivalis, heads a small genus in the amaryllis family. All its kin have bulbs, narrow leaves, and bare flower stalks. Each stalk bears one hanging bell shaped flower at its top. The white flower has six parts, the outer three larger than the inner three. Six anthers open by pores or short slits. The ovary has three cells and ripens into a three celled pod.

The plant is a doubtful native of Great Britain, but it is grown much for market in Lincolnshire. Many forms differ in flower size and in time of bloom. The Crimean kind has broad leaves folded like a fan. Another kind from the Levant has large flowers with a bold green blotch. All kinds grow in most soils and do best left alone.
britannica-1911-spion-kop: Spion Kop is a mountain in Natal, on the north side of the Tugela river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it west of Ladysmith in South Africa. Its name is Dutch for Look out Hill, a common place name in that land. Fame comes from a battle fought there on January 24 in 1900. British forces under Sir Redvers Buller were beaten by the Boers in that fight. The entry notes sharp dispute over the facts and points readers to a Times history of the war.
britannica-1911-sweet-sop:
Sweet-sop is a plant article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a fruit tree of the tropics, also called the sugar apple. Its plant name is Anona squamosa. It is a small tree or shrub with thin leaves and lone greenish flowers. Its fruit is yellow-green, three to four inches across, shaped like a short pine cone.

Inside, the fruit holds a sweet, creamy pulp much like custard. The tree comes from the West Indies and the warm parts of America. It is prized as a fruit and has been carried widely to the eastern half of the world. The article also treats kin species. One is the sour-sop, a small evergreen with a larger dark green fruit whose white juice has a sour tang and is made into a drink.
britannica-1911-top:
Top is the subject of a toy entry in the 1911 Britannica. A top is a toy with a round or cone shaped body. It spins or whirls on a point or peg. Some tops are whipped to keep them moving. Some are spun by a string that unwinds fast. A hollow top hums as it spins, hence its name. Some tops bear bright disks that shift hue as they turn.

The toy is also used in games of chance. In that use it is called a teetotum. Old Greek and Latin texts name the toy more than once. Greek words mark the whipped top and the humming top as two kinds. It notes the toy was known in England by the 1300s. A last note splits the toy word from the word for the upper part of a thing.
britannica-1911-white-thomas-bishop:
Thomas White (1628-1698) was bishop of Peterborough, born at Aldington in Kent. He was schooled at St John's College, Cambridge. After he took holy orders he became vicar of Newark-on-Trent in 1660. He then held posts in London and in Leicestershire. In 1683 he was made chaplain to the princess Anne. In 1685 he was chosen as bishop of Peterborough.

In 1688 White joined Archbishop Sancroft and five other bishops in a plea against the declaration of indulgence of James II. He shared their trial and their glad acquittal. In 1689 he refused to swear loyalty to William and Mary and was stripped of his see. He did not play a large part among the nonjurors after that. White died on 30 May 1698. The article takes care to split him from two other men of the same name.
britannica-1911-wilson-thomas-bishop:
Thomas Wilson, an English bishop who lived from 1663 to 1755, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Burton in Cheshire and educated at Trinity College in Dublin. He was ordained in 1686 and served as curate in Lancashire. In 1692 he became chaplain to the earl of Derby, who in 1697 gave him the bishopric of Sodor and Man.

He was consecrated in 1698, and his long rule in the Isle of Man was marked by reforms. New churches rose, libraries were founded, and books were printed in Manx. His book of the principles and duties of the Christian faith, in 1707, was the first book printed in that tongue. He backed farming and set fruit and forest trees with his own hand.
britannica-1911-worksop:
Worksop is a market town in Nottinghamshire, England, on the Chesterfield Canal, fifteen miles east of Sheffield. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 16,112 in 1901. To the south lies the part of Sherwood Forest known as the dukeries. The church of Saint Mary and Saint Cuthbert is an old priory church. At the Reformation its west part alone was spared, for the use of the parish.

Ruins of a lady chapel and a priory gatehouse from the fourteenth century stand by the church. A manor house in the town was built by the first earl of Shrewsbury. Mary, queen of Scots, lodged there at times in her captivity. Fire gutted the house in 1761. Malting is the chief trade of Worksop. Foundries, tool works, and saw mills add to its work, with a large corn market and fairs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archbishop:
An archbishop, or metropolitan, in the Catholic church today is a bishop ruling a diocese strictly his own. He also presides over bishops of a well-defined district of simple dioceses, but not of provinces. None of those subordinate bishops rule over others; they are called suffragans or comprovincials. The archbishop's personal diocese is the archdiocese, and the district's dioceses together form the metropolitan province.

Some writers wrongly point to Timothy and Titus, Paul's disciples, as the first archbishops. They were probably metropolitans in a wider sense, one for Asia Minor and one for Crete. No exact date can be fixed for the first archbishops in the modern sense. Metropolitans appear as a known institution in the Council of Nicaea in 325, under its fourth, fifth, and sixth canons. The entry traces an office from early custom to settled law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxiliary-bis:
An auxiliary bishop is a bishop deputed to help a diocesan. Help is needed when the diocesan, though able to govern, cannot perform the pontifical functions. It is also needed when his diocese is so large that one bishop's labor cannot cover it. A third case is a court office that keeps him long away. Discipline allows no bishop to be consecrated without title to a diocese, governed actually or potentially.

From that rule flow two classes. Residential bishops, also called ordinary, hold power of order and jurisdiction in their diocese by the pope's grant. Non-residential or titular bishops hold no power over their titular sees. A titular see once had a cathedral, clergy, and people. Pagan occupation or government has left it empty. Its jurisdiction rests with the pope, exercised through Propaganda.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bishop:
Bishop, the office of chief pastor of a diocese, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. From the Greek episkopos, or overseer, through Latin and Old English forms, the title marks a dignitary holding the fullness of priesthood, ruling his portion of the Church under the pope. Catholic faith holds bishops of divine institution.

Powers of order and jurisdiction, election, consecration, visitation, and synods fill the survey, with a defence against Protestant claims that the monarchical episcopate arose only in the second century. The entry argues apostolic origin from Scripture and early witnesses. It is the encyclopedia's fullest statement of what a bishop is.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blenkinsop:
Blenkinsop, a family of Irish-American Catholic publishers, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Peter Blenkinsop, born in Ireland and married to Archbishop Oliver Kelly of Tuam's sister, emigrated from Dublin to Baltimore in 1826 and opened a printing house for Catholic books. Pise's History of the Church in five volumes followed in 1827, and the Metropolitan magazine began in 1830.

His son William, born in Dublin in 1819 and dead at Boston in 1892, studied and taught at St. Mary's College, Baltimore, and carried the family trade forward. The entry presents a father and son who gave American Catholics their own press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boy-bishop:
The boy-bishop custom let a choir or school boy play bishop from Saint Nicholas's Day to Holy Innocents' Day. Chosen on 6 December from monastery schools, cathedral choirs, or grammar schools, he wore pontifical vestments and processed round the parish with companions in priests' robes, blessing the people. He then ruled the church through 28 December, presiding at all offices.

At Salisbury he could even grant vacant benefices, and a boy who died in office received a bishop's funeral honors. Monuments at Salisbury and Lulworth Castle recall boy-prelates, though the Salisbury tomb's genuineness is doubted. Henry VIII ended the custom in 1512, Mary restored it, and Elizabeth ended it again, while the Council of Basle had suppressed it on the Continent in 1431.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-parson:
George Parsons Lathrop, a poet and novelist born at Honolulu in 1851, married into Hawthorne's family and edited his works. Schooled in New York and Dresden, he wed Rose Hawthorne in London in 1871. He served as associate editor of the Atlantic Monthly from 1875 to 1877, then worked Boston and New York papers. His press contributions were varied and voluminous.

In 1883 Lathrop founded the American Copyright League, which won the international copyright law, and helped found the Catholic Summer School of America. He and his wife became Catholics in March 1891. After his death in 1898, his widow, as Mother Alphonsa, founded the Servants of Relief for Incurable Cancer Patients, running two New York cancer hospitals. He also adapted The Scarlet Letter for Damrosch's opera of 1896.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyssop:
Hyssop is a plant named in a few passages of Scripture, which cannot be identified with certainty today. Its presence in Egypt is proved by Exodus, where Moses bids Israel's elders take a bunch of hyssop and sprinkle paschal lamb's blood on door lintels and posts. In the wilderness hyssop was also at hand for sprinkling blood at the sealing of the old covenant.

Mosaic ritual shows hyssop common in Sinai and Canaan and reveals its chief Hebrew uses. Priests sprinkled blood of a sacrificed bird with hyssop to cleanse a person or house touched by leprosy. They also sprinkled water of purification with it to cleanse a tent, person, or vessel polluted by contact with a dead body. The entry surveys those ritual uses and the plant's possible identity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-benedict-b:
St. Benedict Biscop was an English monastic founder, born of a noble Anglo-Saxon family about 628. He died on 12 January 690. This entry follows a youth at the court of Oswy, king of Northumbria. At twenty-five he set out on the first of five pilgrimages to Rome. Back in England, Benedict brought in, wherever he could, the religious rites as he had seen them practised in Rome.

Soon afterwards he set out a second time, pausing on his way home at Lerins in 666 to take the religious habit. Two years later, back in Rome, Pope Vitalian dispatched him with the monk Adrian as advisers to Theodore, the newly appointed archbishop of Canterbury. After two years, in 671, he gave up that office and pilgrimaged to Rome once more. During this and his two later pilgrimages he collected relics, books, and paintings for Wearmouth and Jarrow, founding the former in 674.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-bisho:
William Bishop was the first bishop to lead English Catholics since the old hierarchy died under Elizabeth. Born about 1553 at Brailes in Warwickshire, he died on 16 April 1624. He went to Gloucester Hall, Oxford, in 1570, left abroad four years later, joined Allen at Douay, and finished at Rome. He took orders before returning to England, where arrest, prison, and banishment dogged him. In Paris during exile he earned a Sorbonne doctorate in divinity.

Bishop championed the secular clergy against the regulars' archpriest system, travelling to Rome in 1598 to plead their case, only to face imprisonment at the English College. His 1603 Protestation of Allegiance, signed with thirteen priests, rejected political plots to convert England. Rome at last named him Vicar Apostolic in 1623, and in ten months he set up vicars-general, archdeacons, rural deans, and a chapter of twenty-four canons.
doe-osti-17038073-scorpius-digital-twin-:
Development plan by Will Stem and Mukul Kumar of Lawrence Livermore, dated September 2026, lays out a digital twin for Scorpius, a radiography machine now under construction. Scorpius will take four x-ray images at chosen times and doses, using a multi pulse accelerator powered by nearly one thousand solid state units and about ten thousand control points.

A digital twin is a live computer mirror of the machine, fed by its settings and sensor data. The plan splits that mirror into modules for beam formation, accelerator transport, x-ray making, detection, and image study. Some modules suit real time control, while later ones act as records. The goal is faster tuning once the machine starts running experiments.
doe-osti-17197736-fy-25-progress-on-conc:
Samantha Sabatino and a large Oak Ridge team report fiscal 2025 progress on harvesting irradiated concrete from power plants worldwide, in an August 2025 report. Extending reactor life to 80 years needs better data on the concrete biological shield, which shields radiation and supports the vessel. Most knowledge comes from fast, high dose research reactor tests, not real service, so true samples are prized.

Three efforts anchor the year. From Sweden's Ringhals Unit 2, two unirradiated cores arrived in December 2024 and were read by tomography, x ray methods, diffraction, and petrography. Their mineral mix, rich in quartz and feldspar with pyrite in places, hints at strong expansion risk under radiation. Irradiated cores there await dismantling steps. Canada's National Research Universal reactor shared drawings, dose files, and material records for its shield plugs.
doe-osti-2572284-dichroic-optical-filter:
Technical report LBNL-2001683, dated July 15, 2025, tests whether color filters can sharpen BGO scintillators for time-of-flight PET scanners. The authors are Baharak Mehrdel, Biswajit Das, Youngho Seo, and Javier Caravaca, of UC San Francisco and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. BGO crystals are dense and stop gamma rays well, but their light fades slowly, which blurs timing. Dichroic filters that pass only chosen wavelengths were placed between crystal and sensor.

Filters with cutoffs from 400 to 550 nanometers were tried on detectors read by silicon photomultipliers. The best timing and energy numbers came with no filter at all: 404 picoseconds timing spread and 21.13 percent energy resolution. Among filters, a shortpass at 500 nanometers came closest, at 420 picoseconds. Longpass filters cut signal and timing sharply, worst at 550 nanometers. The result argues for rethinking whether such filters belong in these detectors.
doe-osti-3000612-glovebox-fires-phase-1-:
Anay Luketa of Sandia National Laboratories opens a fire safety study in report SAND2025-13307 on glovebox fires. Gloveboxes, sealed work cabinets with built-in gloves, hold hazardous material work across the nuclear complex. A fire outside one threatens to breach it through glove ports or windows, and planners need to know how long that takes. Phase one checks the simulation tool before any glovebox enters the picture.

The Fire Dynamics Simulator, a fluid dynamics code for fire, was compared with open burner experiments run by New Mexico Tech. Both premixed and diffusion flames were tested, with thermocouples recording the heat. The code tracked the measurements well but ran hot: it overpredicted by about 6 percent for the premixed tests, bias factor 1.06, and about 10 percent for the diffusion tests, bias 1.10. With that known lean, later phases can simulate full rooms with gloveboxes at a cost no test hall could afford.
doe-osti-3003143-ta-54-flanged-tritium-w:
David Patrick Fuehne of Los Alamos National Laboratory summarizes a waste operation's air emissions in report LA-UR-25-31093, issued November 10, 2025. The operation relieved pressure in four flanged tritium waste containers stored at Technical Area 54, some sealed for 18 years. Tritium is radioactive hydrogen, and the containers' internal pressure was a safety concern. This is volume one, covering stack emissions and off-site dose.

The mitigation ran 13 days across September and October 2025. Measured emissions came in far below the bounding levels used in planning, and all doses sat well within Environmental Protection Agency limits. Dose modeling used the CAP88 code with local weather data and a two-meter stack. The author notes the planning assumed worst cases deliberately, since no one had opened this container type after long storage.
doe-osti-3019880-organic-rankine-cycle-i:
Tom Brokaw of ElectraTherm submitted this final report on February 20, 2026, closing award DE-EE0008414. The project ran from 2018 to 2025 in Flowery Branch, Georgia. Its aim was squeezing more electricity from engine exhaust. An organic Rankine cycle bolted onto an engine generator set harvests waste heat the engine throws away. The scope targets: at least 45 percent fuel-to-electric efficiency at full capacity, and 85 percent total combined heat and power efficiency. Ramping from half to full output had to finish within two minutes on grid request.

Over three budget periods, the team developed cycle components and validated a thermodynamic model. The model predicts performance across a temperature and pressure envelope. A working fluid transition to a low-GWP option was identified and validated, and techno-economic analysis closed the work. Grid-responsive gas generation is a niche, but real. The report gives that niche hardware results instead of projections.
doe-osti-3021915-port-technical-assistan:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory proposal paper by Jeriah A. Whitley, Ryan A. Calkins, Shannon K. Idso, and co-authors, dated January 2025, designs a Port Technical Assistance Program that does not yet exist. United States ports face pressure to modernize energy systems, shore power, electrified cargo equipment, cleaner fuels, but hundreds of ports differ wildly in size, cargo, and capacity to plan. The authors argue DOE should offer structured help, drawing on the laboratory's port energy work.

A one-size program will not fit, so the paper proposes categorizing ports and tailoring assistance within a standardized framework. Recommendations cover how assistance would be delivered, how ports would be grouped, and how lessons would spread nationally. The document is a blueprint for decision makers: what the program would do, whom it would serve first, and how it would keep smaller ports from being left behind.
doe-osti-3022091-refining-methods-to-det:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2011723, by J. Wimpenny, tests how reliably laser ablation multi-collector ICP-MS can measure the isotopic makeup of micrometer-sized uranium oxide particles, a measurement used in nuclear safeguards work for the Nuclear Weapons Analytical Laboratory network. Tests on U200 particles show that laser fluence and firing frequency affect the data, and that signal spiking creates anomalous 234U/238U and 236U/238U ratios that no tested setting could eliminate.

The anomalies appear more often in higher-enrichment samples, and of the standards tested only U005-A was anomaly-free. Comparing laser traces for normal and anomalous particles revealed subtle differences, but not ones clear enough to flag bad points among unknowns. The conclusion is blunt: current hardware cannot eradicate the spiking, so the technique needs far more uniform aerosols or faster detector electronics.
doe-osti-3022672-development-of-in-situ-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-21207, by Jack Walton, Alexander Brown, and Daniel Hooks, describes a new capability for watching corrosion happen: digital optical microscopy operated in place during electrochemical testing. Instead of examining a sample only after a polarization experiment ends, the team images the surface while the voltage sweep runs, tying each current change to a visible surface event.

The demonstration case is iron in sodium chloride solution under potentiodynamic polarization. Surface roughness fell in a straight line from 1.8 to 1.2 micrometers over the first 1,000 seconds, the signature of uniform etching. In the final 200 millivolts, current climbed past 50 milliamps, micrographs showed the surface fully covered by corrosion product, and roughness jumped toward 2.0 micrometers as attack localized into pits. The combined record separates uniform corrosion from pitting in a single run.
doe-osti-3025007-laboratory-directed-res:
Roli Gostelow compiled this Oak Ridge National Laboratory volume, ORNL/TM-2026/4474, listing the laboratory-directed research and development projects completed in fiscal year 2025. LDRD is the labs' internal seed funding: small, investigator-led projects that test risky ideas before outside sponsors commit. A completed-projects volume is a census of what that seed money bought in one year across the whole laboratory.

Entries run project by project through Oak Ridge's range. One summarized study built hollow fiber contactors from guanidinium-functionalized material that selectively capture bicarbonate ions from water. The fibers still worked after four adsorption and desorption cycles at salinity like seawater, which the authors read as a case for carbon removal duty from freshwater through brackish and marine water. Hundreds of pages of similar summaries follow the same pattern.
doe-osti-3027393-laboratory-directed-res: LDRD got FY2025-completed again, and this DOE program lists the finished projects. The pages detail the development findings. The researchers get their data. The research was directed. The data were researcher. The FY2025 were projects. The completed were FY2025.
doe-osti-3098117-electric-utility-distri:
Ryan H. Wiser, Galen L. Barbose, Peter Cappers, and colleagues at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory scope out rising local grid costs in this May 2026 slide study. Investor-owned utilities have been spending much more on distribution, the poles and wires that serve streets and homes. The study pulls together trends, drivers, and response options for regulators and policy makers, and it flags where its scope spills past distribution alone.

Five sections cover past and recent cost trends, what drives planned spending, rate and profit requests, and whether current rules reward overspending. One chart tracks return on equity rulings: over the last five years, regulators granted about 95.5 percent of requested returns, a 4.5 percent discount. That is a gentler trim than the 94.0 percent average of 2011 to 2020 or 92.1 percent of 2001 to 2010.
doe-osti-3484506-material-recovery-and-w:
Pacific Northwest plan PNNL-39694 Revision 0, dated August 2026, sets strategy for recovering materials from used nuclear fuel and developing waste forms. Stuart T. Arm wrote the plan. Recovery choices shape both resource use and final waste hazards.

Background sections compare three reprocessing routes: aqueous, electrochemical, and fluoride volatility. Each route gets its own survey of methods and gaps. Mission and strategy sections then set objectives for the program. Planners can weigh fuel reuse gains against waste form needs with the full fuel cycle laid out in one single document. The plan follows used fuel from recovery choices through to final waste forms.
doe-osti-3912524-css-to-phoebus-conversi:
Brookhaven note NSLSII-ASD-TN-454, dated August 31, 2026, records the move of NSLS-II operator screens to a new control platform. Xi Yang is the sole printed author. Screens are leaving Control System Studio for its successor, Phoebus. Yang treats the job as physics-controls work, not screen copying. Workflows and physics behaviour must survive intact, or the move does not count as done.

Under the protocol, screen-local values give way to global signals owned by the controllers. Old Python 2 code is brought up to date, and live actions move into controller logic. Done so far: booster ramp-magnet controls, a light-monitor burst tool, and core beam position tools. Ring tune tools work but await a planned restart before live use. The note fixes decision rules, test stages, and rollback paths, so later moves run the same way.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PictureScoop_Pi: nsia-PictureScoop Picture Scoop: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
maida-s-little-shop:
Maida's Little Shop is a children's story by Inez Haynes Gillmore. Grosset and Dunlap published it, from a 1909 copyright by B. W. Huebsch. Maida Westabrook is a little girl riding from Marblehead to Boston. Her father 'Buffalo,' Dr. Pierce, and her friend Billy Potter ride with her.

Maida is delicate, and her rich father plans a surprise for her. She is to keep a tiny shop of her own in Primrose Court. Chapters follow her first days, her customers, and her small troubles. Halloween, a fair, and Christmas happenings fill her year. Maida learns work, kindness, and courage in her shop. The book was beloved by generations of young girls.
nasa-tm-19650002708-apparatus-for-measur:
C F Smith at Marshall Space Flight Center described, in a July 17, 1964 memorandum, a device for measuring temperature drop across a joint. The joint in question is a bolted interface, where two parts meet. Heat flow changes at such a joint, and designers need real numbers for it.

Smith presents the apparatus itself and how it is used. The aim is a direct reading of the drop across the interface. That kind of measurement helps engineers predict heating in built-up structures. Readers get a concrete test setup, rather than a theory paper.
nasa-tm-19690030673-performance-of-radia:
Denis J. Connolly and Ronald J. Sovie of Lewis Research Center report thruster performance tests in this October 1969 memorandum, TM X-1908. Three radiation-cooled magnetoplasmadynamic arc thrusters were tested: the Avco X-7CR and the McDonnell-Douglas X-4A and X-7. Contractors built all three for NASA Lewis, which ran them at lower pressures than contractor facilities allowed.

MPD thrusters push plasma with electromagnetic forces, and future electric propulsion missions need versions cooled by radiation alone. The Lewis team fired the thrusters inside a long vacuum tank. They measured thrust, arc current and voltage, magnet current, and propellant flow. From those readings they calculated specific impulse and thrust efficiency, then compared results against the contractors' own figures.
sally-bishop:
E. Temple Thurston wrote Sally Bishop, a romance issued in a new and cheaper edition in London in 1912 by Chapman and Hall. United States copyright is dated 1909. A list of Thurston's other books heads the volume, among them The Apple of Eden, Traffic, Mirage, The City of Beautiful Nonsense, and The Garden of Resurrection. The book opens with a letter to Gerald du Maurier. Thurston expects, among other things, the shrug-shoulder smile of critics at his sub-title, a Romance.

In that letter Thurston mocks the canons and rubrics that hedge every act in what he calls the Great World's Fair of Conventionality. Each sideshow there is fenced with the red tape of the Law. Even thieves, he notes, are said to keep honour among themselves. Literature too, he says, has an unwritten canon for the making of books.
susan-clegg-and-her-friend-mrs-lathrop:
Anne Warner's Susan Clegg and Her Friend Mrs. Lathrop was printed at Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1904, under copyrights of 1903 and 1904 held by the Century Company. A prefatory note says the first four chapters ran as separate stories in The Century Magazine during the past year.

The chapters were revised and partly rewritten for the book, and one more, The Minister's Vacation, was added new. Warner warns that Miss Clegg, Mrs. Lathrop, and the rest are wholly imaginary. The stories turn on two gossipy friends in a small town, with Susan's sharp tongue and warm heart driving the talk through neighbors' courtships, church affairs, and small scandals.
the-haunted-bookshop:
Christopher Morley wrote The Haunted Bookshop, and his dedication addresses booksellers with affection and respect. In it, Morley says he meant to write more of Roger Mifflin, whose exploits in Parnassus on Wheels readers had praised. Miss Titania Chapman and a young advertising man then fell in love, and the two of them rather ran away with the tale.

Chapter one, dated from Philadelphia on April 28, 1919, in the dedication, brings the reader to Brooklyn. Morley praises its sunsets and its rows of baby carriages pushed by husbands, then turns toward the bookshop of the title. The book mixes a love story with talk about books, writers, and the trade that sells them.
the-old-curiosity-shop:
Charles Dickens wrote The Old Curiosity Shop, a novel that opens with an old man's night walks through London. The narrator loves the streets after dark, when lamplight shows faces in glimpses and the crowds crossing the bridges pause to look at the water. He muses on the endless tread of feet and the stream of life that never stops.

Dickens uses the walk to set a mood of pity and wonder at city life. The sick man in a narrow court, the beggar, and the pleasure seeker all pass in his mind. The famous novel that follows grew from these walks and the figures met along the way.
the-soul-of-a-bishop:
H. G. Wells follows a bishop through dreams and visions in a novel of nine chapters, moving from wear and tear of episcopacy and insomnia to sympathy, exegesis, and a new world. Chapter one opens inside the bishop's dream, at a scene of bitter disputation in an ancient council.

A hawk-nosed young man argues with a pointing finger while a little rufous man tugs at his robe, and a multitude of heated faces crowds behind them. The emperor commands silence from his golden throne, and old Arius takes up the debate. The assembly stops its ears in staged horror. Then a zealot rushes forward and strikes the old man on the mouth.
yollop:
George Barr McCutcheon published this comic novel in New York in 1922. Chapter one opens with a warning about its hero. Mr. Yollop knows nothing about firearms. Still, he overpowers a burglar and takes the man's loaded revolver. The burglar, dazed and sore, curses Yollop for tackling an armed man at all. Yollop, hard of hearing, keeps demanding that he repeat himself.

The comedy turns on deafness and nerve. Yollop corrects the burglar's speech while holding him at bay. A frontispiece shows the intruder marching Yollop off later, so fortunes plainly reverse. Readers get a farce about a timid man in over his head.
